subsection: 1. Energy requirements and the role of energy

notes.b: Every activity the body carries out, from breathing to running, needs energy, and that energy comes from the food and drink we take in. Knowing what energy is for, and how it is measured, is the starting point for working out how much a person needs.
points: Energy is what the body needs to carry out every function: breathing, circulating blood, nerve and brain activity, growth and repair, movement and keeping warm.
Energy is measured in kilojoules (kJ) or kilocalories (kcal, often called "calories"). 1 kcal is about 4.2 kJ, and food labels give both units.
The body releases energy from carbohydrate, fat and protein, and from alcohol, through chemical reactions, and uses it for every body function.

Energy not needed straight away is stored, because the body cannot waste it: a small store as glycogen (a stored form of carbohydrate) in the liver and muscles, and the large store as fat in adipose tissue (fatty tissue under the skin and around organs).

Three main functions of energy are basal metabolism (keeping the body working at rest), growth and physical activity. Marking schemes also credit the working of the internal organs and the production of heat to maintain body temperature.
notes.tip: If asked for three functions of energy, give basal metabolism, growth and physical activity, and add a short explanation of each.

notes.b: Even when you are lying still, your body is working hard to keep you alive. The energy for this hidden work is called the basal metabolic rate, and it is the biggest part of what most people use each day.
points: BMR is the minimum amount of energy the body needs to stay alive when completely at rest.
It pays for the functions that continue at rest, such as breathing, the heartbeat and circulation of blood, and the work of the brain, liver, kidneys and other internal organs.
It also pays for maintaining body temperature, and for the continuing renewal of cells.

BMR is measured with the person lying at complete rest and awake, in a warm room, about 12 hours after eating (fasting). These conditions mean no movement, cold or digestion adds extra energy use to the result.
For most people BMR is the largest single part of the energy used in a day, more than the energy used for activity.
notes.tip: Use the words "minimum" and "at complete rest" in your definition of BMR. When asked how it is measured, name all three conditions: rest, warmth and fasted.

notes.b: Two people lying side by side will not burn exactly the same amount of energy. BMR varies with the amount and type of body tissue a person has and with the hormones controlling the speed of their metabolism.
points: Age: BMR per kilogram is highest in infancy and childhood because of rapid growth, and it falls with age as lean muscle tissue is lost.
Gender: men generally have a higher BMR than women of the same weight, because men have a higher proportion of lean muscle tissue to fat. Do not say it is simply because they are men.
Body size and weight: the larger the body, the more tissue there is to maintain, so the higher the BMR.
Body composition: lean muscle tissue is more active than fat, so it uses more energy at rest. A muscular person has a higher BMR than a person of the same weight with more fat.

Hormones: the thyroid gland controls the speed of metabolism (the chemical reactions in the body). An overactive thyroid, producing too much thyroid hormone, raises BMR, and an underactive thyroid lowers it.
Health: fever, infection and recovery from injury raise BMR, because the body is working harder to fight illness or repair itself.
Pregnancy and lactation (breastfeeding) raise the requirement, and in a cold climate the body works to stay warm, which raises it too; a hot climate has a smaller effect.
Activity does not change BMR itself. It is a separate part of the total energy the body uses in a day.
notes.tip: Always give a reason with each factor, such as age because of growth and loss of lean tissue. Physical activity is a factor in the total energy requirement but not a factor in BMR, so do not list it when asked about BMR.

notes.b: Building a new body takes energy as well as nutrients. This is why people who are growing quickly need a lot of energy for their size.
points: Energy is needed to build new body tissue, especially muscle, bone, blood and organs.
Infants and young children need a high amount of energy for their size because they are growing quickly.
Teenagers have adolescent growth spurts (short periods of very rapid growth) which raise the requirement sharply.
Teenage boys generally need more energy than girls at this stage because of their greater body size and muscle.
After growth stops, adult energy is needed for the maintenance and repair of tissue, not for new growth.
notes.tip: Growth spurts are credited in questions about teenagers' energy needs, so name them and say they raise the requirement. Boys need more than girls because of greater size and muscle, not just because they are boys.

notes.b: Physical activity is the most variable part of daily energy use, so it is the factor an individual can change most easily.
points: The energy used in activity depends on the type, intensity, duration and frequency of the activity.
Occupational activity: a manual worker, such as a builder or farm worker, or an athlete uses far more energy than someone in a desk job such as an office worker.
Leisure activity: walking, cycling, gardening and playing sport add to daily energy use.
Sedentary lifestyle (little activity and much sitting) means low energy output, so less food energy is needed to meet the body's needs.
notes.tip: Occupation, level of physical activity and sedentary lifestyle are all credited as factors, so name the job or activity and say whether it raises or lowers the requirement.

notes.b: A person's daily energy requirement is more than their BMR. It adds the energy for activity and for dealing with food, and then rises or falls with circumstances such as climate, pregnancy and health.
points: Total daily energy use is made up of BMR, plus the energy for physical activity, plus the small amount used to digest, absorb and process food (the thermic effect of food). BMR on its own is not the total requirement.
Occupation: manual and athletic work increases the requirement, while sedentary work lowers it.
Climate: in cold conditions the body burns more energy to keep its temperature stable, partly through the muscular work of shivering, so energy needs are higher than in a warm climate.
Pregnancy: extra energy is needed for the growth of the baby and the placenta and for the mother's added tissue, especially in the later months.
Lactation: extra energy is needed to make breast milk.
Health: fever, illness, burns and recovery from injury or surgery raise energy needs. Prolonged bed rest lowers the activity part of the requirement.
The factors examiners list are age, gender, body size or weight, occupation, level of physical activity, climate, pregnancy, lactation, health or illness, growth spurts, sedentary lifestyle and BMR.

When a person is described, such as a teenager who plays sport, a builder, an office worker, a pregnant woman or an older retired person, name the factor, say whether it raises or lowers the requirement, and give the reason.
notes.tip: Never just list factors. Give each one a because, saying whether it raises or lowers the requirement: for example, growth spurts raise it, a sedentary lifestyle lowers it and a cold climate raises it. Do not mix up BMR, the minimum at rest, with the total requirement, which adds activity and digestion.

keyTerms.definition: The minimum energy the body needs at complete rest to keep vital functions and body temperature going.
A metric unit of energy; 1 kcal is about 4.2 kJ.
A unit of energy still used on food labels; 1 kcal is about 4.2 kJ.
Muscle, bone and organ tissue, which uses more energy at rest than fat tissue does.
Hormones from the thyroid gland that raise the rate at which the body uses energy.
The amount of energy a person needs each day to balance their energy use and maintain health.
The energy the body uses to digest, absorb and process the food it eats.
A way of living with little physical activity, so that daily energy output is low.

factCards.term: Four body functions that use energy at rest
factCards.definition: Breathing; circulation of blood by the heart; activity of the brain and internal organs; maintaining body temperature.
The person lies completely still and awake in a warm room, after a fast of about 12 hours.
Age; gender; body size and lean muscle mass; thyroid hormones.

factCards.term: Two effects of a cold climate on energy needs
factCards.definition: The body produces more heat to keep its temperature stable, so energy use rises; shivering, a muscular response, also uses extra energy.

factCards.term: Two extra energy needs in pregnancy and lactation
factCards.definition: Growth of the baby, placenta and mother's extra tissue during pregnancy; production of breast milk during lactation.

factCards.term: Three main components of daily energy use
factCards.definition: BMR; energy for physical activity; energy used to digest and absorb food.

questions.prompt: Outline two factors that affect the basal metabolic rate of an adult.
questions.model: Age: BMR is highest during growth and falls with age because lean muscle tissue declines, so an older adult needs less energy at rest. Gender: men generally have a higher BMR than women of the same weight because they have more lean muscle tissue and less fat. Body size and composition, pregnancy and thyroid hormones are also accepted, with a brief explanation of how each one changes BMR.

questions.prompt: Discuss the factors that determine the total daily energy requirement of a teenager who plays competitive sport.
questions.model: BMR: a teenager has a high BMR because of growth and lean muscle development, and boys generally have a higher BMR than girls of the same weight. Growth spurts raise energy needs further. Physical activity: competitive training has high intensity, long duration and high frequency, so energy for activity is a large share of the total. Thermic effect of food: a larger amount of food eaten to meet the demand also raises the energy the body uses to digest it. Climate: training in cold or hot conditions changes the energy used to maintain body temperature. Health: illness or injury lowers activity and so reduces requirements until recovery. Intake should match these needs so that energy balance is maintained.
